analysis.one_liner: Bans Congress from delegating lawmaking to agencies, voiding any rule not fully written by Congress.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one senator with zero cosponsors in June 2012, died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit Congress from delegating any legislative power to federal agencies, the President, the courts, states, or any other body. Any new rule, regulation, or presidential directive affecting the public could only take effect if it was authorized by a statute that itself contains no delegation. Any existing law, rule, or regulation that did not comply would have no force or effect, no legal, civil, or criminal action could be brought under it, and private citizens could sue the federal government to block its enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: The bill is framed as serving citizens by requiring that all binding federal law come from elected members of Congress rather than unelected agency officials. In practice, its immediate beneficiaries would be regulated businesses: the bill would strip enforcement power from nearly every federal rule and regulation not spelled out line-by-line in a statute, which covers most of modern federal regulation — environmental, workplace, food, and financial rules among them.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any Act of Congress from delegating legislative power to any agency, the President, the courts, any state, or any other organization or individual.
Bars any new presidential directive, rule, or regulation governing private activity unless it is authorized by an Act of Congress that itself contains no delegation of legislative power.

Declares that any noncompliant law, rule, or regulation has no force or effect, bars all legal, civil, or criminal action under it, and gives aggrieved persons the right to sue the United States for an injunction against enforcement.
Requires the Comptroller General to report to Congress identifying all prior statutes that contain prohibited delegations, with the aim of phasing them out.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who relies on federal protections carried out through agency rules — clean air and water standards, food and drug safety, workplace safety, financial and consumer rules — because those protections are enforced through rules written by agencies under broad statutes, and the bill would strip them of force 90 days after enactment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal rules and protections

drawbacks.text: The bill would void enforcement of virtually the entire modern federal regulatory framework, because Congress writes broad statutes and agencies fill in the technical standards; the bill's own enforcement clause strips any noncompliant statute, rule, or regulation of all force 90 days after enactment.

Congress cannot write every technical standard in detail, and courts since the early 1800s (as the bill's own findings note, citing Wayman v. Southard) have allowed some delegation; the bill provides no replacement process, leaving large parts of federal law unenforceable.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the scale: the Comptroller General's required report would identify essentially every regulatory statute Congress has passed since the late 1800s, meaning a full re-legislation of the administrative state with no transition plan.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The principle behind the bill — that only elected lawmakers should make binding law — has genuine appeal, and the bill's findings make that case at length. But as written, the remedy is to invalidate enforcement of nearly all federal regulation at once, with nothing to replace it. Consumers, workers, and the public would lose enforceable protections while businesses gained sweeping relief from federal rules. The bill offered no transition beyond a Comptroller General report.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in June 2012, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the Write the Laws Act in the Senate on June 28, 2012.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it remained in committee until the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal rules — air and water standards, food and drug safety, workplace protections, financial safeguards — kept them, because the bill that would have stripped their enforcement died without a vote. Regulated industries did not get the broad relief from federal regulation the bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Write the Laws Act and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party split can be measured; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses (manufacturers, energy, financial firms, and other industries subject to federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would have voided enforcement of nearly all federal rules not fully written into statute, giving regulated industries sweeping relief from federal oversight. The public's cost would be the loss of the same rules that protect air, water, food, workplaces, and finances.

Agencies would lose the power to promulgate or enforce any binding rule not fully defined by statute. Because agency rulemaking is the mechanism through which most federal protections are actually carried out, the agencies' retained authority runs alongside the public's interest in enforcement.
